actions.justification: Mandatory first action. Patient has HR 105, BP 195/110, SpO2 93%, RR 22 - all abnormal and require immediate formal assessment and continuous monitoring per AHA guidelines.
Mandatory - AHA Class I recommendation to obtain 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact to evaluate for STEMI. Critical to confirm working diagnosis before any treatment.

Mandatory - Immediate history is essential for risk stratification. The combination of chest pain, right hemiparesis, severe headache, and hypertension raises concern for aortic dissection or hemorrhagic stroke, which would significantly alter management and contraindicate anticoagulation/thrombolytics.

MANDATORY: Immediate cath lab activation is critical to achieve door-to-balloon time <90 minutes. Primary PCI is preferred over thrombolytics especially given the neurological symptoms (hemiparesis, headache) which may represent concurrent stroke — thrombolytics would be contraindicated, making PCI the only reperfusion option.
MANDATORY: Aspirin 325mg chewable is Class I recommendation for STEMI. Antiplatelet therapy is required as adjunctive therapy for primary PCI.
SpO2 is 93%, below the 94% threshold — supplemental oxygen is indicated to correct hypoxia in this STEMI patient.

MANDATORY: P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel/ticagrelor) is required as adjunctive antiplatelet therapy for STEMI per AHA guidelines. Must be given before/at time of primary PCI. Already 30 minutes into presentation with door-to-balloon target of <90 min.

MANDATORY: Anticoagulation with heparin or enoxaparin is required for STEMI management per AHA guidelines to prevent thrombus propagation and support PCI. Time-critical given door-to-balloon deadline.

Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy for STEMI when performed within 90 minutes. Currently at 30 minutes post-arrival; cath lab activated. Must formally arrange PCI immediately to meet door-to-balloon target. Patient also has neurological symptoms (hemiparesis, headache) which require urgent cardiology input during PCI planning.

IV access is essential for medication delivery including anticoagulation, antihypertensives, and emergency drugs. Critical in this hemodynamically complex patient with BP 195/110 and neurological symptoms.

Urgent cardiology consultation needed given complex presentation: anterior STEMI with concurrent right hemiparesis and severe headache in a severely hypertensive patient with AF. Need expert input on managing competing risks of reperfusion therapy vs. possible intracranial/aortic pathology causing neurological symptoms.

Baseline high-sensitivity troponin required per AHA guidelines for STEMI workup to confirm myocardial injury and provide trending data for ongoing management. Serial troponins will help assess infarct size and reperfusion success post-PCI.
ECG interpretation is needed to confirm anterior STEMI pattern, assess for additional ST changes, arrhythmias (patient has known atrial fibrillation), and guide ongoing management decisions.

Patient has HR 105 and severely elevated BP 195/110. Beta-blocker is indicated in STEMI to reduce heart rate, myocardial oxygen demand, and manage hypertension — provided no contraindications such as acute decompensated heart failure or severe bronchospasm. Use with caution given SpO2 93%.

Patient has ongoing acute chest pain. Morphine may be considered for pain relief if pain is not controlled, though should be used judiciously given potential adverse effects in STEMI and the neurological presentation requiring careful monitoring.
Comparing with prior ECG can help characterize the extent and acuity of ST changes in this anterior STEMI presentation, supporting clinical decision-making for the cath lab team.

Although this is an anterior STEMI, obtaining right-sided leads helps rule out concurrent RV involvement before considering any nitrate therapy, especially given severely elevated BP (195/110) and the need to avoid hypotension in RV infarction. Also important given the complex neurological presentation.

Patient has severely elevated BP (195/110 mmHg) and ongoing chest pain. Right-sided ECG (V4R) has already been obtained to rule out RV infarction. Nitrates are indicated for symptom relief and BP management while awaiting primary PCI. Note: the concurrent neurological findings (right hemiparesis, severe headache) require urgent neurology/stroke team evaluation alongside STEMI management.

Door-to-balloon time has reached 90 minutes and PCI may be delayed. However, this patient has significant contraindications to fibrinolysis including severe hypertension (BP 195/110), acute neurological deficits (right hemiparesis, severe headache suggesting possible hemorrhagic stroke or aortic dissection), and elevated troponin. Clinical team must weigh these contraindications carefully - fibrinolysis is likely contraindicated given the neurological presentation, but consideration and documentation of this decision is warranted per STEMI guidelines when PCI delay is a concern.

Patient has SpO2 93% and elevated HR 105, with hypertension but potential need for cautious fluid support. This patient also has neurological symptoms (right hemiparesis, severe headache) raising concern for concurrent stroke or hypertensive emergency — careful fluid management is warranted. This is the only available action not yet completed.

Patient has SpO2 of 93% and elevated HR of 105 with BP 195/110. While mandatory STEMI actions are complete, the patient has neurological symptoms (right hemiparesis, severe headache) alongside STEMI — intravascular volume support may be warranted. This is the only remaining available action and provides supportive care while awaiting PCI.

Patient with anterior STEMI, elevated troponin (5.8), hypertension (BP 195/110), AF, and neurological symptoms (right hemiparesis/headache suggesting possible concurrent intracranial event) requires CCU-level monitoring after cath lab activation.

Risk stratification is indicated given complex presentation with STEMI, severely elevated BP, AF, and possible acute neurological event (stroke/ICH) which may alter management decisions including anticoagulation and reperfusion strategy.

Given the complex presentation with concurrent neurological symptoms alongside STEMI, formal assessment for early invasive strategy timing and appropriateness should be documented, particularly since BP is 195/110 and there may be a contraindication to thrombolytics.
